title: July 2026: England's driest July since 1836
body:
England recorded 6.5 mm of rain in July 2026. Not in a week — in the whole month. That is 10% of what a normal July brings, and it is the driest July in a record that began in 1836. The previous record, 13.4 mm set in 1911, was beaten by more than half.

Southern England had 1.9 mm. Three per cent of average. It is the driest month of any name that southern England has ever recorded.

Alongside that, the UK had its sunniest July on record, and England and Wales had their sunniest calendar month ever observed — not just their sunniest July, their sunniest month full stop. Wales had its joint warmest July on record and England its second warmest.

And then there is Scotland, which had a pleasant summer month and broke nothing at all.

That contrast is what this article is about: how one weather pattern, sitting over the whole country at once, produced an all-time record at one end of the island and an ordinary warm month at the other.

**What actually happened, nation by nation**

Here are the Met Office figures for the month, measured at weather stations on the ground.

Rainfall, as a share of the 1991–2020 average: England 6.5 mm (10%), Wales 9.3 mm (9%), Northern Ireland 26.9 mm (30%), Scotland 72.0 mm (69%). The UK as a whole finished on 28.9 mm, 35% of normal.

Sunshine: England 305.6 hours (156%), Wales 308.0 hours (174%), Northern Ireland 194.2 hours (143%), Scotland 178.6 hours (127%). The UK total was 258.7 hours, 149% of average.

Average temperature: England 19.2 °C (2.8 °C above normal), Wales 17.8 °C (+2.5), Northern Ireland 16.4 °C (+1.8), Scotland 14.5 °C (+1.1). The UK average was 17.4 °C, 2.1 °C above normal.

Read down those lists and the pattern is the same every time. Every part of the UK was drier, sunnier and warmer than normal. But England and Wales were off the end of the scale, while Scotland was simply having a nice summer. In the Met Office's own words, Scotland was the only nation not to come close to breaking records.

Nothing was cold anywhere. Nothing was wet anywhere. The difference across the country was one of degree — and the degree was enormous.

**The cause: a lid of high pressure**

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/08f6ae5dd_July2026Pressure.PNG|Air pressure through July 2026 compared with the July average. The whole map is red, meaning pressure was high everywhere, and it is almost the same shade from Shetland to Cornwall — the same block of high pressure sat over every part of the country at once.]]

Air pressure is simply the weight of the atmosphere pressing down on you. When it is high, air is sinking. When it is low, air is rising. That distinction decides almost everything about British weather, because rain can only form in rising air — as air rises it cools, and cooling air cannot hold its moisture, so cloud forms and rain falls. Sinking air does the reverse: it warms, it dries out, and it clears the sky.

Through July, pressure over the UK averaged around 1020 millibars against a July norm of about 1014. Six millibars above average may not sound like much, but pressure normally swings by 20 millibars or more within a single week as Atlantic storms pass through. For a whole month to average this high means those storms were largely absent. They tracked far to the north of Scotland or stalled out in the Atlantic instead of crossing us.

Meteorologists call this a blocking high: an area of high pressure that parks itself and refuses to move, forcing the usual procession of Atlantic weather systems to go around it. July 2026 was a textbook example, and it lasted almost the entire month.

Now look at the colour of that map. It is virtually the same shade everywhere. The high pressure was not stronger over England than over Scotland. So the cause was evenly spread across the country — which makes the wildly uneven result the thing that needs explaining.

**Why the same high pressure did different things in different places**

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/35e2f249a_July2026Wind.PNG|The direction the wind blew from most often at each point during July. Britain's usual summer wind comes from the south-west; this month it came from the north-west instead. The arrows also differ across the country, sitting closer to due west over southern England and further round to the north over Scotland.]]

A block of high pressure is not a uniform thing. It has a centre, where air sinks hardest and skies are clearest, and it has edges, where the sinking is weaker and passing weather systems can still clip the outside.

England and Wales spent the month near the centre. Scotland spent it near the northern edge. That is the whole explanation, and the wind map is the evidence for it.

Britain's normal summer wind blows from the south-west, at roughly 244 degrees on a compass. That matters because air arriving from the south-west has crossed thousands of miles of warm Atlantic and arrives loaded with moisture. It is where most of our rain comes from.

Through July 2026 the wind averaged 301 degrees instead — from the north-west. That is a shift of nearly 60 degrees, and it changes the character of the air completely. North-westerly air has taken a shorter, cooler route from the north Atlantic, and crucially it is descending as it feeds into the high. Descending air does not make rain.

The arrows are not the same everywhere, and that is the detail worth catching. Over southern England they sit closer to due west, deep inside the sinking core of the block. Over northern Scotland they point more sharply from the north-west, out on the rim, where the weakened remains of Atlantic weather systems were still able to slide past the top of the block. Scotland's 72 mm of rain is what leaked in around that northern edge.

One weather pattern. Two very different places to be standing in relation to it.

**Rainfall: the gradient across the island**

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/a4aa33e40_July2026Rainfall.PNG|Rainfall compared with the July average. The deepest browns across England, Wales and Ireland mark the areas furthest below normal; the north-west of Scotland is the palest part of the map, meaning it came closest to a normal month. Note that the map is built from a computer model of the atmosphere and is less extreme than the ground measurements — the shape of the pattern is what to read here, not the exact numbers.]]

The map shows a steady gradient from the driest ground in the south-east to the least dry in the north-west, and it lines up with the station measurements underneath it.

At the extreme end, southern England's 1.9 mm is close to no rain at all. A single ordinary shower delivers more than that. To go a full summer month with essentially nothing, in a country whose climate is built around Atlantic rainfall, is genuinely without precedent in nearly two centuries of measurement.

The north-west of Scotland comes closest to normal, and there is a reason it always does in situations like this. The Highlands are high ground standing directly in the path of moist air coming off the Atlantic. Air forced to climb over mountains has no choice but to rise, and rising air cools and drops its moisture regardless of what the pressure pattern is doing. It is the one rain-making mechanism that keeps working when the weather systems have gone. Everywhere downwind of the hills gets the leftover air, now sinking and dried out.

The timing of the rain in the Highlands supports this. In the model data, roughly twice as much rain fell there in the six hours around midnight as in the six hours of the afternoon. Ordinary summer showers work the other way round — they are powered by the sun heating the ground, so they peak in mid-afternoon and fade after dark. Rain that prefers the middle of the night is not being made by the sun. It is being made by the hills, which work just as well at 2am.

**Temperature: warm everywhere, exceptional in the south**

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/a01735ccf_July2026Temperature.PNG|Temperature compared with the July average. The deep reds across southern England, the Midlands and Ireland mark the largest excesses. The model behind this map shows parts of north-west Scotland near or slightly below normal, but the Met Office's station measurements put Scotland as a whole 1.1 °C above average — where the two disagree, the ground observations are the ones to trust.]]

England averaged 19.2 °C, 2.8 °C above normal and its second warmest July on record. Wales at 17.8 °C was 2.5 °C above and equalled its warmest July ever. Scotland reached 14.5 °C, 1.1 °C above normal — a warm month, but nothing remarkable.

The UK-wide figure of 17.4 °C sits in the middle and describes almost nowhere. It is the average of an English record and a Scottish shrug.

The reason for the warmth follows directly from the sunshine. Under a blocking high the sky stays clear, so day after day the sun heats the ground without interruption, and that heat accumulates through the month. This is warmth manufactured locally by sunshine rather than warm air blown in from somewhere hotter. It also explains why the warmth tracks the sunshine so closely: England got the most sun and the most heat, Scotland the least of both.

One honest caveat about this map. The computer model it is drawn from puts parts of north-western Scotland at or a little below the July average. The Met Office's actual thermometers say Scotland finished 1.1 °C above. Models of this kind are known to struggle over mountainous coastal ground, and the measurements win. Read the map for the shape of the pattern — hottest in the south, least hot in the north-west — and not for the exact value at any one spot.

**Sunshine and cloud: the clearest skies ever measured**

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/4d3ef7552_July2026Sunshine.PNG|Sunshine compared with the July average. Every part of the UK was sunnier than normal; the golds mark where the excess was greatest. Wales reached 174% of its average and England 156%, while Scotland, still well above normal, reached 127%.]]

[[img:https://base44.app/api/apps/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/files/mp/public/69945c97e07811f2b5427aa6/a0a686df4_July2026Cloudiness.PNG|Cloud cover compared with average. Orange marks skies clearer than normal. It is close to a mirror image of the sunshine map, which is exactly what should happen — two separate measurements agreeing is a sign the pattern is real rather than a quirk of one dataset.]]

This is where the month is most extraordinary. England and Wales did not merely have their sunniest July — they had their sunniest month of any kind since records began. Wales managed 308 hours of sunshine, 174% of a normal July. England had 305.6 hours.

For context, that is roughly ten hours of sunshine every single day for thirty-one consecutive days.

The cloud map is worth looking at beside the sunshine map, because the two are measured in completely different ways and they agree. Where sunshine is high, cloud is low, in the same places by the same amounts. When two independent measurements tell you the same story, the story is real.

Every nation was sunnier than usual, including Scotland at 127%. Once again the difference across the country is one of degree rather than direction — which is precisely what a single block of high pressure sitting over everyone should produce.

**Why a record-breaking summer is not simply good news**

The rainfall and sunshine records are two halves of the same problem. Strong sunshine pulls moisture out of soil, crops and reservoirs through evaporation. Normally rain replaces it. In July 2026, across England and Wales, almost nothing did.

That combination drains water from the landscape from both ends at once, and it does so fastest in exactly the wrong place. Southern and eastern England hold the least water in reserve, draw the most from rivers and underground supplies, and grow the most thirsty crops. They are also the areas that recorded 3 to 10% of normal rainfall.

Scotland, the part of the country that came nearest to a normal month, is the part with the most water to spare.

**How a pattern like this ends**

Blocking highs break down in one of two ways. They can fade gradually, as the Atlantic jet stream shifts back south and the usual sequence of weather systems resumes. Or they can be broken from underneath, when a pocket of cooler air finally pushes in below the accumulated heat and forces it upward — which ends things suddenly, in thunderstorms rather than in drizzle.

Early August is leaning towards the second. The forecast data behind this site models pressure around 7 millibars below normal on 4 August, with temperatures still about 4 °C above average and daily rainfall well above normal: hot, humid air being undercut, which is the standard recipe for a thundery breakdown. By around 11 August the models rebuild high pressure again, dry and settled.

So the pattern that produced this month is bending, not gone.

**A note on where these numbers come from**

Every national statistic quoted here — rainfall, sunshine, temperature and the records themselves — comes from the Met Office's provisional July 2026 climate summary, measured at weather stations across the UK. Those are the authoritative figures and the ones to quote.

The maps are produced by this site from a global weather model of the atmosphere rather than from rain gauges. Such models are excellent at showing the shape and position of a weather pattern, which is what they are used for here, but over the UK they tend to smooth out extremes: this one puts UK rainfall at 48% of average where the gauges recorded 35%, and sunshine at 114% where the gauges recorded 149%. Where a map and a measurement disagree, the measurement is right.

Sources: Met Office, "Historic July sees record dryness, unprecedented sunshine and exceptional warmth", and the Met Office July 2026 regional statistics.

title: Introducing News: the story behind the forecast
body:
Welcome to News — a new section of MyWeather Website for the weather that needs more than a symbol and a number.

A forecast page is very good at telling you what is going to happen. It is far less good at telling you why, how confident anyone is, or whether the thing that just happened was unusual. That is what this page is for.

**What you will find here**

Stories are tagged so you can see at a glance what kind of piece you are getting:

- Analysis — a closer look at a setup: why the models disagreed, what the ingredients actually were, what tipped it one way
- Storm — coverage of active or imminent severe weather, and what it did once it arrived
- Climate — how a month or a season actually turned out against the long-term average, rather than how it felt
- Forecast — the thinking behind a forecast, including where the uncertainty sits
- Update — changes to the site itself, like this one

**Why it exists**

The honest reason is that the interesting part of forecasting rarely fits in a tile. A yellow thunderstorm warning tells you there is a risk. It does not tell you that the models had been arguing about it for three days, or that the whole thing hinged on how quickly the cloud broke that morning.

When a forecast goes well, it is worth explaining what the signal was. When it goes badly — and it sometimes will — it is worth explaining that too. Verification is not much use if nobody ever writes up what it showed.

**Charts and graphics**

Stories can carry the graphics produced in the MyWeather graphics tools: monthly climate anomaly maps, synoptic charts, weather-type maps, storm outlooks. Where a piece is making a claim about rainfall or temperature against the average, expect to see the map it came from rather than just the number.

**A note on the figures**

Where a story quotes a percentage against the long-term average, it is measured against the 1991–2020 baseline. Where a figure is indicative rather than exact, it will say so on the page. Anything drawn from reanalysis rather than observations will be labelled, because the two do not always agree and pretending otherwise helps nobody.

**How often**

There is no fixed schedule. Stories go up when there is something worth saying — an active spell of severe weather, a month that broke from the pattern, a change to the site worth explaining. Quiet weeks will be quiet.

The newest story is always at the top, and any piece can be linked to directly, so a story worth sharing can be sent on its own.

title: What's new on MyWeather: forecasts, symbols and warning maps
body:
A run of changes has landed across MyWeather over the past few days. Most of it is visible the moment you open the site, so here is what has changed and why.

**Location forecasts are back**

You can search any UK town or city again and get a full forecast: hour by hour for the next two days, then a seven-day outlook. Temperature, feels-like, wind and gusts, rainfall chance, humidity, pressure, visibility and UV are all there, with the hourly detail expanding underneath each day.

The data comes from the Met Office site-specific forecast, which is the same source behind their own point forecasts. It covers the UK only — search somewhere outside it and the page will say so plainly rather than quietly showing you nothing.

**Every weather symbol has been redrawn**

The full set has been rebuilt from scratch: sun, moon, cloud, rain, drizzle, showers, sleet, hail, snow, fog, mist, wind and thunder, at every intensity.

They now work as a set rather than a collection. Intensity reads consistently — a heavy rain symbol looks as heavy as a heavy snow symbol, so scanning a week actually tells you something. Showery conditions keep the sun or moon visible beside the cloud, because that gap is the difference between a bright day with bursts of rain and a grey day that never lets up. Continuous conditions show unbroken cloud.

Each symbol animates briefly when it first appears — rain falls, flakes drift, bolts strike — and then settles into a still, complete picture. It draws the eye once and then gets out of the way.

**The sky behind the forecast**

The forecast page background is now a drawn sky rather than a flat colour wash. Sun and moon with proper glow, cloud banks drifting at different depths, lightning that strikes in bursts and lights the cloud around it, fog that shears as it moves, and rain and snow falling across it.

It follows whichever day you have selected, so moving through the week changes the weather behind the numbers. It also follows the time of day, shifting through sunrise, daylight, sunset and night.

**Warning maps show the real warning area**

This is the change with the most work behind it. Warning maps had stopped displaying anything at all — the map the site was pulling from had gone, and the failure was silent, leaving an empty box.

They now draw the actual warning area as issued: the exact shape, matched to the specific warning rather than approximated from the counties it covers. If a warning covers half of one county and none of its neighbour, that is what you will see.

**Past warnings tell you how they ended**

A warning that ran its full course and one the Met Office withdrew early are different things, and the past warnings list now says which. Expired means it ran to its published end time. Cancelled means it was called off before it got there — the threat did not materialise.

Cancelled warnings previously vanished from the list entirely, which made a withdrawn warning look like it had never been issued.

**More to come**

This is not the end of it. There is more in progress, and further changes will show up here as they land — each one written up in this section rather than appearing unannounced.

If something looks wrong, it is worth saying so. Several of the fixes above came from exactly that.

title: TCM V3 — THE END OF AN ERA  -  An Official TCM Announcement
body:
Today marks the end of one of the most significant chapters in the development of TCM.

After extensive work to diagnose and resolve the ongoing data and data-display problems affecting TCM V3, I have reached the decision that the time has come to officially close this chapter and move the project forward.

TCM V3 is officially retired, effective immediately.

This is a major milestone for TCM. V3 has been an important part of the project's development, but its role in the evolution of TCM has now come to an end.

THE DECISION

The problems affecting TCM V3 have been investigated through numerous attempts to identify their underlying cause and restore the system to a dependable state.

Despite those efforts, I have not been able to establish a solution that would give me enough confidence to continue developing V3 as a reliable model.

Rather than continuing to pour development time into an increasingly difficult system with no clear resolution, I have decided to close V3 and redirect that effort into the future of the project.

This means there will be no further attempts to revive, repair, or continue expanding TCM V3.

The decision is final.

CLOSING THE V3 CHAPTER

Every major development project reaches a point where moving forward becomes more valuable than continuing to maintain what came before.

For TCM, that point has now arrived.

V3 represents a significant stage in the project's history. It was part of the process of developing the ideas, systems, and approaches that have shaped where TCM is today.

Its retirement therefore is not simply the removal of an old model.

It represents the conclusion of a development era.

The work carried out during V3 has provided experience, exposed limitations, and helped establish a clearer understanding of what needs to be achieved in the next generation.

That experience will now become part of the foundation for what comes next.

FROM V3 TO V5

With V3 now behind the project, development attention is moving decisively towards TCM V5.

V5 is being treated as a new generation of TCM rather than a continuation of the existing V3 system.

The development philosophy is different, the ambitions are greater, and the amount of work being put into the next generation is considerably broader.

The goal is to build a system that is more capable, more sophisticated, and better equipped for continued development over the long term.

Most importantly, the lessons learned from previous versions are being used throughout the development process.

TCM V5 is the opportunity to take the project in a completely new direction.

BEHIND THE SCENES

A considerable amount of TCM V5 development is already taking place privately.

While much of that work has not yet been publicly shown, the coming weeks will begin to change that.

More information will be released about the development of V5, alongside previews, demonstrations, screenshots, and showcases of different parts of the system as they become ready to be presented.

These updates will provide a much clearer look at what is being built and where the project is heading.

Some parts of the development will remain private, but progressively more of V5 will be brought into view.

PRIVATE DEVELOPMENT

For now, TCM V5 will remain private.

Access is currently limited to selected individuals while development and testing continue.

This gives the project the space to evolve without treating every development build as a finished public release.

It also allows changes to be made where necessary as the model develops, without creating the expectation that every experimental feature or early version represents the final product.

The current V5 environment should therefore be viewed as an ongoing development programme rather than a finished public model.

THE FIRST PUBLIC RELEASE

There will eventually be a public version of TCM V5.

However, that release will happen only when the first complete version of the model has been properly finished.

There is no intention to release V5 simply to put a new version in the hands of the public.

The first release needs to represent a genuine milestone in the project's development and provide a solid foundation for everything that follows.

That means the model will continue to undergo development, testing, refinement, and evaluation before that point is reached.

The priority is not speed.

The priority is building the right first version.

WHAT THE NEXT FEW WEEKS WILL LOOK LIKE

The end of TCM V3 now allows the project's attention to move almost entirely towards the next generation.

That means the coming weeks will be focused heavily on TCM V5 development and showcasing.

Expect to see more updates, more behind-the-scenes material, and more demonstrations of the work being carried out.

Some announcements may introduce individual features or developments, while others will provide a broader look at the direction of the project.

For those who have been following TCM for a long time, this will be the beginning of seeing the next stage of the project take shape publicly.

A THANK YOU FOR THE V3 ERA

Before closing this chapter, I want to thank everyone who followed TCM throughout the V3 era.

Whether you tested the model, viewed its forecasts, provided feedback, supported development, or simply watched the project evolve, you became part of this stage of its history.

Development is rarely a straight line.

There are successful ideas, failed ideas, unexpected problems, breakthroughs, setbacks, and lessons that only become clear through experience.

TCM V3 has been part of that process.

And although V3 is now ending, the knowledge gained from developing it will continue forward.

THE NEXT CHAPTER

Today, TCM V3 closes its chapter.

Tomorrow, development continues with V5.

This is not the end of the TCM project.

It is the point where the project leaves one generation behind and begins building the next.

The V3 era has given TCM a foundation of experience.

TCM V5 is where that experience is put to work.

There is still a long road ahead, and the first public release is still some way off.

But the next generation is already being built.

TCM V3 — Retired.

TCM V5 — In Development.

The next chapter starts now.
